\chapter{Keeping Well}
\label{ch:te-keeping-well}
\hlchaptermodality{93}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask whether someone is keeping well, say I am comfortable and happy, and name aches in the body.}

Complete TE-C93-body: good news and bad news about how you are.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kṣēmaṁ]{\te{క్షేమం} (kṣēmaṁ) — wellbeing, safety}

\label{lesson:TE-C93-wellbeing}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Telugu for a wound, then the Telugu for weakness.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{క్షేమం}}
\textbf{\te{క్షేమం}} (\emph{kṣēmaṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}wellbeing, safety\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\te{క్షేమంగా} \te{ఉన్నారా}?} — \textquotedblleft{}are you keeping well?\textquotedblright{}, a warmer, more formal cousin of \textbf{\te{బాగున్నారా}?}, heard from elders and read at the top of letters.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A respectful way to ask after someone.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kṣēmaṁ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kṣēmaṁ}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} ask \emph{kṣēmaṁgā unnārā?}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Telugu for a wound, then the Telugu for weakness, then say \emph{kṣēmaṁ} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{క్షేమం} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Wellbeing, safety\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hāyigā]{\te{హాయిగా} (hāyigā) — comfortably, pleasantly}

\label{lesson:TE-C93-comfortably}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Telugu for weakness, then the Telugu for wellbeing.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{హాయిగా}}
\textbf{\te{హాయిగా}} (\emph{hāyigā}) — \textquotedblleft{}comfortably, pleasantly\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\te{హాయిగా} \te{ఉంది}} — \textquotedblleft{}it is pleasant\textquotedblright{}, said of a cool breeze, a good rest, an easy day.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word for when things are good.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Telugu for weakness, then the Telugu for wellbeing, then say \emph{hāyigā} again

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[sukhaṁ]{\te{సుఖం} (sukhaṁ) — comfort, ease}

\label{lesson:TE-C93-ease}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Telugu for wellbeing, then the Telugu for comfortably.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{సుఖం}}
\textbf{\te{సుఖం}} (\emph{sukhaṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}comfort, ease, contentment\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\te{సుఖంగా} \te{ఉన్నారా}?} — \textquotedblleft{}are you comfortable?\textquotedblright{}, a host's question. Its opposite is the \textbf{\te{కష్టం}} you already have: ease against difficulty.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Ease, set against a word you know for its opposite.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sukhaṁ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sukhaṁ}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} ask \emph{sukhaṁgā unnārā?}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Telugu for wellbeing, then the Telugu for comfortably, then say \emph{sukhaṁ} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{సుఖం} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Comfort, ease\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[santōṣaṁgā]{\te{సంతోషంగా} (santōṣaṁgā) — happily, gladly}

\label{lesson:TE-C93-gladly}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Telugu for comfortably, then the Telugu for comfort.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{సంతోషంగా}}
\textbf{\te{సంతోషంగా}} (\emph{santōṣaṁgā}) — \textquotedblleft{}happily, gladly\textquotedblright{}.

It is \textbf{\te{సంతోషం}}, the \textquotedblleft{}pleased\textquotedblright{} of your first introductions, with \textbf{-\te{గా}}. \textbf{\te{సంతోషంగా}} alone answers a request: \textquotedblleft{}gladly\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
An old word put to a new job with the ending you know.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{santōṣaṁgā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{santōṣaṁgā}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} answer a request with \emph{santōṣaṁgā}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Telugu for comfortably, then the Telugu for comfort, then say \emph{santōṣaṁgā} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{సంతోషంగా} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Happily, gladly\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[oḷḷu]{\te{ఒళ్ళు} (oḷḷu) — the body}

\label{lesson:TE-C93-body}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Telugu for comfort, then the Telugu for gladly.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{ఒళ్ళు}}
\textbf{\te{ఒళ్ళు}} (\emph{oḷḷu}) — \textquotedblleft{}the body\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\te{ఒళ్ళు} \te{నొప్పులు}} — \textquotedblleft{}body aches\textquotedblright{}, with the plural of \textbf{\te{నొప్పి}}. What a fever leaves behind.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Well, comfortable, at ease, glad, and the body that aches when you are not.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{oḷḷu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{oḷḷu}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{oḷḷu noppulu}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Telugu for comfort, then the Telugu for gladly, then say \emph{oḷḷu} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
